passage:
I'm Hemant, and I wanted to tell you properly, Ramesh sir, because you asked why I stopped coming to the running club.
When we moved here in June I didn't know anyone. Then some seniors invited me to the Circle. It started with morning runs, and it was brilliant. They knew my name on the first day. Wristbands, a chant before every run, "brother" this, "brother" that. For the first time here I felt like I belonged.
Then it changed. Five a.m. meetings, then weekends. Last week the leader told me my old friends from class "hold me back". And he said, "Don't tell your parents about the Circle yet. They won't get it."
That made my stomach go cold.
You listened to all of it, sir, and you didn't laugh. You said wanting friends was completely normal, and hiding a group from my family was the warning sign. Then you called my mum while I was still sitting here.

qa.q: What did the leader say about Hemant's old friends from class?
qa.a: The leader said Hemant's old friends from class "hold me back".

qa.q: Why did the Circle feel so good to Hemant at first?
qa.a: Hemant had moved in June and knew nobody, so being known by name, the chant and being called "brother" gave him a strong feeling of belonging.

qa.q: What was the turning point that made Hemant ask for help?
qa.a: Being told not to tell his parents about the Circle made his stomach go cold, and he recognised the secrecy as a warning and went to Ramesh sir.

qa.q: How does Ramesh sir respond to what Hemant tells him?
qa.a: Ramesh sir listens without laughing, tells Hemant that wanting friends is normal and that hiding a group is the warning sign, and calls Hemant's mum that same day.

grounding: A lonely teenager is drawn into an intense group offering quick friendship and rituals, recognises the danger when told to hide it and cut off others, and tells Ramesh sir.

passage:
Nilesh and I have been in the same hostel wing since Class 8, so I noticed when he changed.
This term he started leaving the common room early for "calls with the group". He wore the same grey thread on his wrist every day. He started saying "the awakened" and "sleepers", and when I asked who the sleepers were, he said, "People like you, Tenzin. No offence."
He laughed differently, sort of far away. He stopped coming to Saturday football. I think he was lonely after his best mate left in April, but I don't know that for sure.
Then last Thursday I saw a message on his screen: "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."
I went to Mrs D'Souza, our house parent, that evening. She listened, thanked me and said telling was right. Before dinner she sat with Nilesh in her office for a long time, and she called his parents that night.

qa.q: What did the message on Nilesh's screen say?
qa.a: It said, "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."

qa.q: What does Tenzin think might be behind Nilesh's change, and how sure is Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin thinks Nilesh may have been lonely after his best mate left in April, but openly says it is only a guess.

qa.q: Which moment made Tenzin act, and was it the right step?
qa.a: The message telling Nilesh to hide the chat from his warden; taking it to the house parent that same evening was right because secrecy is the warning sign.

qa.q: How does Mrs D'Souza respond once Tenzin tells her?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza listens, thanks Tenzin, sits with Nilesh in her office before dinner and calls his parents that night.

grounding: Tenzin notices a hostel-mate drawn into a secretive group with rituals and new words, and reports it once the group demands secrecy; the house parent acts the same day.

passage:
I'm Zubin. When we moved to Pune in Class 10, I didn't know a single person. Lunch was the worst part.
Then some older students invited me to "the Circle". Music, long talks on a terrace, everyone hugging when you arrive. Within a week they knew my birthday and my favourite song. It felt amazing to be wanted.
There were rules, though. Phones in a basket. White threads on our wrists. After a month the leader said, "Your old friends drag you down. And don't tell your parents about us yet; they wouldn't understand."
That line stuck in me like a splinter. That night Vishal, my best friend from back home, messaged: "you've gone quiet, you ok?" I realised I'd been ignoring him for weeks.
I went into the kitchen and told Mum everything. She put her tea down, listened without interrupting, and said, "Wanting friends is not wrong. Asking you to keep secrets from us is." She called the school counsellor right then and set up a meeting for the next day.

qa.q: What did the leader say about Zubin's parents?
qa.a: 'Don't tell your parents about us yet; they wouldn't understand.'

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when the Circle first welcomed Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin felt wanted and happy after lonely lunches, so the quick hugs and the remembered birthday felt amazing.

qa.q: Which warning sign did Zubin notice, and what was the wise step?
qa.a: Being told to drop old friends and keep the group secret from parents; telling Mum that same night, and Mum calling the school counsellor at once.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal during those weeks?
qa.a: Vishal was being ignored by a best friend for weeks and noticed the silence, which is why the 'you ok?' message came.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager drawn to an intense group with rituals and quick warmth, and recognising the demand to cut off friends and keep secrets.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B, Thursday
For three weeks Jeevan, who used to sit alone at lunch, has been glowing. He talks about his "crew" from an online group: daily 5 am check-ins, a special greeting, older members who call him "brother". I was glad at first. He needed friends.
This week things changed. He stopped sitting with Lokesh, his one friend in class. Lokesh told me Jeevan said the crew wants him to "cut off anyone who doesn't get it". Today, when I asked where the crew meets in person, Jeevan would only say it was "secret for now".
What I did: I spoke with Jeevan at break, calmly. I told him wanting a group is completely normal, but real friends don't ask you to drop other people or keep secrets from home. He looked relieved, and a bit scared. With him beside me, I called his mother the same afternoon and informed the school counsellor, who will see him tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Lokesh say the crew wants Jeevan to do?
qa.a: To 'cut off anyone who doesn't get it'.

qa.q: How did Jeevan seem when the teacher spoke to him at break?
qa.a: Jeevan looked relieved and a bit scared, as if part of Jeevan had been waiting for someone to notice.

qa.q: What did the class teacher do that protected Jeevan?
qa.a: Spoke calmly, said wanting a group is normal but secrecy and cutting people off are not, then called Jeevan's mother that afternoon and informed the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Jeevan stopped sitting together at lunch?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt hurt and worried at being dropped, and cared enough to tell the teacher what the crew had said.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a lonely teenager drawn into an online group with rituals and quick friendship, and acting on the push to cut off others and keep secrets.

passage:
Sunday night
The Rise group had their weekend retreat today. I've been going for two months. Before that I was the new kid nobody picked for anything. At Rise, people clap when you walk in. Bhaskar sir says we're "chosen".
Today he said something that's still sitting in my stomach. We have to stop "wasting time" with people outside, and the retreats are "not for parents' ears". Everyone nodded. So did I.
On the bus back, Amandeep texted: "Missed you at cricket again. Everything ok?" I nearly didn't reply. That scared me more than anything.
When I got home I told Papa. I thought he'd be angry. He wasn't. He said, "I'm glad you found people who make you feel welcome. But anyone who needs you to hide them is not safe." He's calling the school counsellor first thing tomorrow and says I don't have to go back next weekend.
Texted Amandeep: "Cricket Tuesday?"
Nitin

qa.q: What did Bhaskar sir say the retreats were not for?
qa.a: The retreats are 'not for parents' ears'.

qa.q: What scared Nitin on the bus back?
qa.a: Nitin felt scared on noticing how close Nitin came to ignoring Amandeep's message, a sign of already drifting away from old friends.

qa.q: What did Papa say and do that helped?
qa.a: Papa stayed calm, said wanting to feel welcome is fine but a group that must be hidden is not safe, and planned to call the school counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Nitin's text about cricket?
qa.a: Amandeep, who had been missing Nitin at cricket, would likely feel relieved and glad to have the friend back.

grounding: Shows a teenager who felt out of place drawn to a group offering applause and belonging, then recognising the push to hide it and cut off others.
